Description:
Body of a male lying in a flexed position. 
Skull - Detached at the level of the disc-space between cervical vertebra 6 and cervical vertebra 7. No obvious fractures. All teeth present. Mouth closed. Some tufts of hair remain on the scalp, and some linen bandages are on the face and body surface. 
Thorax and Abdomen - Grit and sand in both cavities. Many of the ribs are fractured. No abnormal changes in the intervertebral discs but there are gross osteo-arthritic changes with lipping involving the lumbo-dorsal spine. 
Long Bones - The left arm and hand are attached to the body, but there is a spiral fracture of the shaft of the left humerus. The remainder of the limbs are dislocated and the bones severely fractured. The legs appear to be encrusted with a mixture of mud of gravel. There is a small exostosis arising from the medial aspect of the upper end of the left tibia. No lines of arrested growth are visible.;
Curators Comments:

Object type: human skeletal remains (object name); coffin (object name)
Description:
Skeleton of an adult, sex unknown, lying in a flexed position on the left side in a cane basket.
Skull -  No obvious fractures. All teeth probably present. Mouth gaping. 
Thorax and abdomen -  Many of the ribs are dislocated at the costo-vertebral junction, but not fractured. The spinal column is dislocated in the lower dorsal region and there are well-marked osteo arthritic changes with associated lipping in the lumbar region. No abnormal changes in the intervertebral discs.
Long bones -  No definite fractures seen. The right foot is dislocated. Lines of arrested growth at the lower ends of tibiae.
Remains of a coffin of basketwork: just large enough to contain a contracted burial. The reeds used for the sides and ends of the coffin were bound into bundles before final assembly. All the upper part of the coffin is missing. The remaining parts, with the bones, were consolidated with paraffin wax by the excavator.;
Dimensions: 117.00 centimetres coffin ;  158.00 centimetres skeleton ;  58.50 centimetres coffin ;
Bib references: Spencer 1980 / Early Dynastic Objects; Dawson & Gray 1968 / Catalogue of Egyptian Antqiuities in the British Museum: Mummies and Human Remains; Fletcher, Antoine and Hill 2014 / Regarding the Dead: Human Remains in the British Museum

Object type: human skeletal remains (object name); coffin (object name)
Description:
Skeletal remains of a young adult, sex unidentified, with wooden coffin.
Skull - Some of the lower front teeth show evidence of attrition. The cranium in its dimensions appears to be within normal limits. 
Thorax, Abdomen, Arms, and Legs: - The body is reduced to a mass of disjointed bones, now held together by paraffin wax. Remains of charred linen bandages are visible.
A rectangular coffin for a contracted burial: made of rough planks fastened together by dowels. Some of the boards, particularly those of the lid, were not cut with parallel edges but were trimmed to fit irregular spaces. The coffin was constructed by making a frame of narrow bars of wood, forming the edges of the coffin and the corner posts, and then filling in the spaces with thin planks, set vertically along the sides and horizontally at the ends. The cover was made of rough planks laid lengthwise. Some parts of the lid are missing, but the surviving woodwork is in good condition.;
Dimensions: 48.50 centimetres coffin without lid ;  91.20 centimetres coffin ;  56.20 centimetres coffin ;

Description: Statuette of a king:  the figure of a beardless king wearing a white crown, the weight of which seems to be pushing out the tops of his huge ears. Wrapped in a short, stiff robe, he strides forward on his left leg. Perhaps the most striking aspect of the figure is the sense of age conveyed by the stoop of the king's shoulders, the forward thrust of his neck, and the droop (possibly somewhat exaggerated by weathering) of his long, pointed chin. Though a few would disagree, most believe that this is a depiction of an aged king. The robe is the type worn by kings during the sed-festival. This ceremony of royal rejuvenation was already in existence at the beginning of the First Dynasty. Here, the garment has the form of robes shown on other Early Dynastic representations of this ceremony. Unlike other versions of the robe, however, the material is patterned, with a design of diamond shapes bordered by two bands of guilloche. The designs were carved with such plasticity that even the under-and-over intertwining of the strips in the guilloche bands can still be seen. The effect strongly suggests woven designs in a heavy fabric, rather than painting on leather, as has sometimes been suggested. The most singular feature of the robe is a sort of flap that hangs down over each shoulder. These "epaulets" are worn and cracked and extremely hard to see, but the better-preserved example, on the left shoulder, apparently has a  scalloped edge. The objects appear to be unique, and no one has yet come up with a satisfactory identification or explanation, apart from a tentative (and unlikely) suggestion that they might represent animal paws. The arms of the figure are held at the front, by the fold of the cloak, and it is possible that the band of the robe hung over the right hand.;

Description: A terminal from a piece of furniture: formed of a piece of sheet copper beaten out into a bell-shape, with the wide end closed by a separate copper disc. The object has been restored from fragments and is heavily corroded. It still contains traces of decayed wood.;
Curators Comments:
This kind of terminal was used on chairs and beds, and was sometimes made of ivory as an alternative to copper-cased wood, (W. B. Emery, 'Great tombs of the First Dynasty; excavations at Sakkara' II' (London, 1954), 44, no.105; 45, nos. 165-7 and pl.XXVII). In Saqqara, tomb 3471, copper-cased terminals were discovered in situ on a wooden bed-frame (W. B. Emery, 'Great tombs of the First Dynasty; excavations at Sakkara' I (Cairo, 1949), 57 and pl.11A). The same kind of terminal occurs on the bed of Hetepheres, but in this case covered with gold (H. S. Baker, 'Furniture in the Ancient World' (London, 1966), 47, fig. 35.) For parallels, see W. B. Emery, 'Great tombs of the First Dynasty; excavations at Sakkara' II' (London, 1954), 39, no. 25; 40, no. 42; 45. no. 176; 54, no. 303 and pls.XXVI-XXVII; W. B. Emery, 'Excavations at Saqqara, 1937-1938 : Hor-aha' (Cairo, 1939), 64, no. 349; W. M. F. Petrie, 'Royal Tombs of the Earliest Dynasties' II, pls.XXXV, 83; XLI, 87; E. Amélineau, ‘Les Nouvelles Fouilles d’Abydos’ I (1895-6), pl.IX. See also the representations of terminals on furniture, J. E. Quibell,  'Excavations at Saqqara, 1911-12 : the tomb of Hesy' (Cairo, 1913), pls.XIX-XX; H. S. Baker, 'Furniture in the Ancient World' (London, 1966), 31-2, figs. 18-20.
Bibliography:
W. B. Emery, 'Great tombs of the First Dynasty; excavations at Sakkara' III (London, 1958), 50, no. 4.

Description: Part of an ebony oil label: restored from two fragments, with a hole for attachment at the top right-hand corner. The front surface bears an incised inscription, arranged vertically on the left side and in four horizontal registers on the right. These four registers are bordered by a large 'rnpt' hieroglyph, indicating that the text records the events of a particular year. The top register bears a scene of the Sed-festival, showing the king wearing the double crown, running as part of the ritual and seated on a throne in a booth.  The meaning of the lower registers is not entirely clear, but they include references to the destruction of a stronghold and the taking of captives.;
Inscription:
Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: front Inscription script: hieroglyphic Inscription translation: Titles/epithets include : Seal-Bearer of the King of Lower Egypt Inscription note: Incised. The vertical inscriptions give the name of Den and of the seal-bearer of the King of Lower Egypt, Hemaka, together with the name of another official, Iti-sen (P. Kaplony, 'Die Inschriften der Ägyptischen Frühzeit I (Wiesbaden, 1963), 438), who bore the title mḏḥty-nsw (Kaplony reads this title mḏḥ-mḏḥ(w) nsw, see 'Die Inschriften der Ägyptischen Frühzeit I (Wiesbaden, 1963), 300). Beside his name are two signs of uncertain reading (P. Kaplony, 'Die Inschriften der Ägyptischen Frühzeit I (Wiesbaden, 1963), 439; ibid., II, 1004 (note 1607). This official seems to have been associated with the ḥwt-nsw and another building, which may have been an oil-press (P. Kaplony, 'Die Inschriften der Ägyptischen Frühzeit II (Wiesbaden, 1964), 1005-7, n. 1610) . Beneath the king's name is the designation of the kind of oil to which this label referred ( 'Die Inschriften der Ägyptischen Frühzeit I (Wiesbaden, 1963), 313. The name of the oil is sṯỉ- Ḥr), together with its quantity, although part of the number is missing.
On the right of the label, the inscriptions in the four registers are bordered by a large 'rnpt' hieroglyph, indicating that the text records the events of a particular year. The top register bears a scene of the Sed-festival, showing the king wearing the double crown, running as part of the ritual and seated on a throne in a booth (Vikentiev believed that the scene represented two booths superimposed, with the king wearing the white crown in one and the red crown in the other, 'Annales du Service des Antiquitiés de l'Égypte' 41 (1942), 288-9; 'Annales du Service des Antiquitiés de l'Égypte' 48 (1948), 682-4). The meaning of the lower registers is not entirely clear, but they include references to the destruction of a stronghold and the taking of captives. For discussion, see R. Weill R. Weill, ‘Recherches sur la première dynastie et les temps prépharaoniques' I (Cairo, 1961), 16-37; II, 90-2; J. Vandier, 'Manuel d'Archeologie egyptienne', I, (2), 853-5; Sthe, 'Untersuchungen' III, 66-7; F. Legge, ‘Proceedings of the Society of Biblical Archaeology’ 29 (London, 1907), 101-5.;
Bib references: Spencer 1980 / Early Dynastic Objects; Strudwick 2006 / Masterpieces of Ancient Egypt

Inscription type: inscription Inscription script: hieroglyphic Inscription translation: Anedjib and his nsw-bỉtỉ name, Merpabia. Also the name of a building. Inscription note: The reading of the name of the building which also occurs on the seal is not entirely certain, but it probably represents a palace in Lower Egypt, if the signs under the name of the building are to be read mḥyt.
Kaplony suggests the reading ḥwt p Ḥr w‘ỉ nsw bỉd Mrỉ pw bỉʒ and gives strong arguments for interpreting the building as the royal palace of Buto (P. Kaplony, 'Die Inschriften der Ägyptischen Frühzeit II (Wiesbaden, 1964); 816-17, 858-61, 1126). Helck also believes the building to be a palace, but reads ḥwt p Ḥr msnw 'Mansion of the throne of Horus the harpooner' (W. Helck, ‘Untersuchungen zu den Beamtentiteln des ägyptischen alten Reiches’ (Gluckstadt, 1954), 32-3). See also the comments of Newberry, ‘Proceedings of the Society of Biblical Archaeology’ 34 (London, 1912), 280-1; Weill, ‘Recherches sur la première dynastie et les temps prépharaoniques' I (Cairo, 1961) , 125-36; Griffith, in Petrie, Royal Tombs of the Earliest Dynasties' I, 44; P. Lacau & J. P . Lauer, 'Pyramide à degrès’  IV, fasc. 2, 37. This building occurs on many inscriptions of the First and Second Dynasties; see the examples collected by Kaplony, 'Die Inschriften der Ägyptischen Frühzeit' II (Wiesbaden, 1964); 1224 (page references given there), and those in Lacau-Lauer, 'Pyramide à degrès' IV, fasc. 2. 9-11, 21-2, 37.;

Description:
Ivory label for a sandal: It is well-preserved and restored from three fragments, with a hole for attachment at the top right-hand corner. The two lower corners have been cut off at an angle. On the front surface is an incised scene showing the king Den with an upraised mace, about to strike a captive. The king's name is written before him, in the centre of the top of the label. He wears a bull's tail, symbolic of fertility and ferocious power. Instead of a crown, however, Den wears an archaic version of a royal headcloth, with the rearing neck and head of a royal uraeus cobra at his forehead. 
That the enemy is an Easterner is indicated by his long locks and pointed beard, which resemble those on later depictions of Asiatic foes. On the right is the  standard of Wepwawet and an inscription. Behind the figure of the king are three signs giving the name of the official Inka. The reverse side of the label bears an incised picture of a pair of sandals, indicating the type of object to which the label was attached.;
Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription script: hieroglyphic Inscription translation: First Occasion of Smiting in the East Inscription note: Incised.; Inscription type: inscription Inscription script: hieroglyphic Inscription transliteration: jnkʒ Inscription translation: Inka Inscription note: Incised. Probably to be understood as the name of an official. See P. Kaplony, 'Die Inschriften der Ägyptischen Frühzeit I (Wiesbaden, 1963), 423.; Inscription type: inscription Inscription script: hieroglyphic Inscription translation: Den Inscription note: Incised. Another group of three hieroglyphs in front of the king are of uncertain meaning. Possibly the signs could be read 'tm.sn', or 'They shall not exist', referring to Egypt's enemies as represented by the captive.. The form of the sign at the top of the group is not a very good rendering of 'tm', however.;
Bib references: Spencer 1980 / Early Dynastic Objects; Parkinson 1999 / Cracking Codes: The Rosetta Stone and Decipherment; Russmann 2001 / Eternal Egypt: Masterworks of Ancient Art from the British Museum; MacGregor 2010 / A History of the World in 100 Objects; Vandenbeusch 2024 / Pharaoh: art and power in ancient Egypt

Description: A heavy pear shaped mace-head: of hard crystalline limestone, pierced vertically for fixing to a handle. The surface originally had fifteen small square projections, of which only three are relatively intact. Between these projections the  mace is decorated with a design of a snake in low relief, coiled symmetrically around the object, with the head and the tail represented close together. Beneath the topmost group of projections, and between the coils of the snake, are four figures of birds also in relief. The whole object is carved with great delicacy and detail, and is well preserved apart from the damaged projections and a small amount of chipping at the base.;
Curators Comments:
For maces with such projecting bosses, see the writing of the name, Aḥa-nakhte in F.LI. Griffith and P. E. Newberry, 'El-Bersheh' II (London: 1893-4), pl.XV.
The exact form of these birds is not clear; possibly they are the hieroglyph 'wr'.
Location: On display (Room 64 - Early Egypt, Display Case 6)

Part of a green glazed composition tile: decorated with ribbed lines. The only edge to remain unbroken is covered with a blue glaze of a paler shade than the green of the ribbed face. The tile's upper side is convex, and it is pierced to facilitate its attachment to a wall.;
Curators Comments:
This tile was found in debris associated with the early Osiris Temple at Abydos, but has no specific context. It is interesting to note that, while the tile is green, the unbroken edge displays a light blue colour.  
Precisely what  this  tile  decorated  at Abydos is unknown because no tiles have been found in situ, but it is quite likely that the walls of the sanctuary and nearby shrines were decorated in the same manner as the niches of Djoser's funerary complex.
For parallels, see W. M. F. Petrie, 'Abydos' I (London, 1902), pl. LIII, 20-2; W. M. F. Petrie, 'Abydos' II (London, 1902-4), pl. XI, 237; A. Scharff, ‘Die Altertümer der Vor – und Frühzeit Ägyptens’  (Berlin, 1929-31), no. 367 and pl. 38.
Bibliography:
W. M. F. Petrie, 'Abydos' I (London, 1902), pl. LIII, 19.
Bib references: Spencer 1980 / Early Dynastic Objects; Friedman 1998 / Gifts of the Nile: Ancient Egyptian Faience

Description: Game piece in the shape of a lion: the figure of a crouching lion has lost its front legs and been blackened by fire, but the details of the carving are very well preserved. The animal is male; his mane and his chest and belly hair are depicted in relief as a series of overlapping scallops carved in considerable detail but with very little plasticity. His tail runs up the centre of his back and ends in a curve to the left. His open mouth, bared teeth, and creased muzzle suggest that he is snarling. This ivory lion was used as a gaming-piece, and it shows signs of considerable wear on the underside, as well as on each side where it was held.;
Bib references: Spencer 1980 / Early Dynastic Objects; Russmann 2001 / Eternal Egypt: Masterworks of Ancient Art from the British Museum

Description: Broad rectangular axe-head: with concave butt and gently convex sides, which turn out slightly at the corners of the cutting edge. As one of the sides is more convex and shorter than the other, the cutting end, which is moderately convex, is a little lop-sided. The blade has been cleaned since its acquisition; previously it was thickly corroded on one face, where the surface is now pitted. The same face has a number of fine cracks, which are probably the result of the process of manufacture. Except for small surface imperfections and a gash on one side, the other face is in excellent condition. Marks of the original hammering are plainly visible on the cutting edge, which is quite sharp and shows distinct signs of wear. The better-preserved face of the axe bears a motif or inscription in hieroglyphs, executed in a punched pointille technique, consisting of three separate elements.;
Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription script: hieroglyphic Inscription note: Punched. Uncertain reading. The inscription may well be a personal name, perhaps similar in form to the name sr-ỉnpw known from an Early Dynastic stela from Abydos. P. Kaplony, 'Die Inschriften der Ägyptischen Frühzeit’ I (Wiesbaden, 1963), 628.;
Curators Comments:
See E. Kühnert-Eggebrecht, Die Axt als Waffe und Werkzeug im Alten Ägypten' (Berlin, 1969), 13, 98 and pl. 1, 3, where this form of axe is called type B-I. For parallels, see ibid., 98 and references.
The date of acquisition suggests that this object may have come from the Early Dynastic royal tombs at Abydos.
For other examples of inscribed Early Dynastic axes, see W. M. F. Petrie, 'Tools and weapons : illustrated by the Egyptian collection in University College, London' (London, 1917), pl.III, 103-4.
Bib references: Spencer 1980 / Early Dynastic Objects; Davies 1987 / Catalogue of Egyptian Antiquities in the British Museum

Description: Rectangular ivory or bone label: blackened by burning and slightly broken at the top right-hand corner, where there was a hole for attachment. The front surface is inscribed.  The reverse side of the label bears a single incised sign.;
Inscription:
Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: obverse Inscription script: hieroglyphic Inscription translation: Djer Inscription note: Incised. The serekh is facing right, and the left of it is a representation of a walled enclosure, probably intended for the royal palace of Buto (ḥwt Ḥr p w‘ỉ or ḥwt Ḥr p msn) See P. Kaplony, 'Die Inschriften der Ägyptischen Frühzeit I (Wiesbaden, 1963), 385. Kaplony suggests the reading ḥwt p Ḥr w‘ỉ nsw bỉd Mrỉ pw bỉʒ and gives strong arguments for interpreting the building as the royal palace of Buto (P. Kaplony, 'Die Inschriften der Ägyptischen Frühzeit II (Wiesbaden, 1964); 816-17, 858-61, 1126). Helck also believes the building to be a palace, but reads ḥwt p Ḥr msnw 'Mansion of the throne of Horus the harpooner' (W. Helck, ‘Untersuchungen zu den Beamtentiteln des ägyptischen alten Reiches’ (Gluckstadt, 1954), 32-3). See also the comments of Newberry, ‘Proceedings of the Society of Biblical Archaeology’ 34 (London, 1912), 280-1; Weill, ‘Recherches sur la première dynastie et les temps prépharaoniques' I (Cairo, 1961) , 125-36; Griffith, in Petrie, Royal Tombs of the Earliest Dynasties' I, 44; P. Lacau & J. P . Lauer, 'Pyramide à degrès’  IV, fasc. 2, 37. This building occurs on many inscriptions of the First and Second Dynasties; see the examples collected by Kaplony, 'Die Inschriften der Ägyptischen Frühzeit' II (Wiesbaden, 1964); 1224 (page references given there), and those in Lacau-Lauer, 'Pyramide à degrès' IV, fasc. 2. 9-11, 21-2, 37.

 Above the building is a hieroglyph which has been variously interpreted. Kaplony suggests the reading kḍ 'build' ('Die Inschriften der Ägyptischen Frühzeit' I (Wiesbaden, 1963), 285), but Weill interprets the sign as 'the perch' of the divine falcon (‘Recherches sur la première dynastie et les temps prépharaoniques I (Cairo, 1961), 131).; Inscription type: inscription Inscription note: Incised. Sign of uncertain reading, but which probably represents the kind of object to which this label was attached, probably some kind of stave or baton.;
Location: On display (Room 64 - Early Egypt, Display Case 10)

Description: A small grey slate bangle: roughly oval in section, with convex outer face. Curators Comments:
Chamber M seems to have been used as a rubbish hole: the objects in it were generally damaged. The latest pottery and flints date to the reign of Peribsen and the jewellery is not likely to be much earlier.

Description: Thirteen small rectangular glazed composition plaques: including two fragments, from inlay work. All are in good condition and in only one case has the blue glazed composition decayed to white. Perhaps from a wall.;
Dimensions: 1.59 centimetres object marked with identification numbers ;  1.40 - 1.60 centimetres;  0.24 centimetres object marked with identification numbers ;  0.15 - 0.25 centimetres;  1.14 centimetres object marked with identification numbers ;  0.90 - 1.20 centimetres;
Curators Comments:
The thirteen small tiles were recovered from a storage chamber of a large elite tomb of the First Dynasty. Little survived the tomb's destruction, but fragments of wooden furniture were found in the same magazine. The rectangular shape, small size,  and thin profile of each glazed composition piece suggest that they once embellished a box or piece of furniture as inlay.
Bibliography:
W. M. F. Petrie, 'Royal Tombs of the Earliest Dynasties' II, 44, no. 160 and pl. XXVII (only 13 of the 16 plaques illustrated are in the British Museum);
W. B. Emery, 'Great tombs of the First Dynasty; excavations at Sakkara' II' (London, 1954), p. 44, no. 160 and pl. 27.
Bib references: Spencer 1980 / Early Dynastic Objects; Friedman 1998 / Gifts of the Nile: Ancient Egyptian Faience

Description: A small piece of gold casing: probably intended as an amulet or to hold an inlay of some other material. The object is made from two pieces of thin gold, beaten together into a curved hollow bar, open at the front; at each end of the bar the metal has been rounded off so as to bring the opposite sides together.;
Curators Comments:
This object is very similar to the gold horns on a 'Bat' amulet from Abydos; Cairo JE 28169 (Cf. C. Aldred, ‘Jewels of the Pharaohs’ (London, 1971), pl. 25; A. Wilkinson, 'Ancient Egyptian Jewellery' (London, 1971), pl. 1A; XIXA, B). Representations of the 'Bat' worn as a girdle pendant occur as early as the reign of Narmer, but no example has been found in excavations. See A. Wilkinson, 'Ancient Egyptian Jewellery' (London, 1971), 21.
Also from this tomb: bracelet bead (1901,1012.28).

W. M. F. Petrie, 'Royal Tombs of the Earliest Dynasties' II (London, 1901), 24, 36, pl.VIA, 19;

Bib references: Andrews 1981 / Catalogue of Egyptian Antiquities. Jewellery I; Spencer 1980 / Early Dynastic Objects

Description: An ivory leg from a bed or chair: carved in the form of a bull's foot. The top is marked with scratches where the ivory has been sawn and there is a hole in the middle of the top surface for attachment. Two more holes, each 0.7cm in diameter, are pierced horizontally through the upper part of the leg, from one side to the other. The surface of the piece has been carved with care, details of the veins being shown on one side, and it has been polished. At the base, the hoof rests on a low pedestal with decoration in the form of narrow horizontal grooves. There is a shallow depression cut into the underside of this pedestal.;
